div.head: Editorial Introduction
div.p: This digital edition presents Ella C. Evanson’s “Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda,” a typescript narrative preserved in the Ella Evanson Scrapbooks held by University of Washington Libraries Special Collections. Produced in Seattle in the early 1940s, the text emerges from the wartime classroom culture of Washington School, where Evanson taught students from diverse racial backgrounds. The story centers on a Chinese student, Ming Chin, and his classmates’ efforts to raise funds for a baby giant panda. At the same time, its references to China, Japan, war, and classroom conflict place the story within the broader context of World War II and the racial tensions that shaped Asian American life on the West Coast.

Our edition treats “Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda” not only as a children’s story, but also as a social and archival artifact. The narrative preserves traces of classroom life, wartime feeling, racial language, and the ways global conflict entered the everyday world of students. As Yoon K. Pak argues in Wherever I Go, I Will Always Be a Loyal American, Seattle’s Japanese American schoolchildren experienced a painful contradiction between democratic citizenship education and the racial exclusion authorized by Executive Order 9066. Although Evanson’s story focuses on a Chinese student, its classroom setting and its reference to anti-Japanese language make it important for understanding the racialized atmosphere of Seattle schools during the war.

Our editorial approach is primarily diplomatic. We preserve original spelling, punctuation, capitalization, grammar, and historically charged language rather than modernizing or sanitizing the document. We use TEI markup to identify people, places, historical references, and key terms, while editorial notes provide historical and archival context. This apparatus is designed to help readers understand the story as both a literary text and a record of wartime student experience and local Asian American history in Seattle.

div.head: Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda
div.p: James Smith strutted up to the front of the schoolroom and said, "Miss Brown, may I make an announcement?"
"Yes, certainly, James."

"As treasurer of the Baby Giant Panda FundDuring the late 1930s and early 1940s, the acquisition of a live giant panda from China became a major cultural event in American zoos, often accompanied by large-scale public fundraising campaigns initiated by children. The efforts of the students in the story reflect this real historical “panda craze,” and the content announced by the teacher highlights how the outbreak of the Pacific War suddenly ended these trans-Pacific cultural and diplomatic exchanges., I wish to report that the last penny is in and now we can pay for our baby giant panda."

The noisy applause that followed was offset by the report of Miss BrownBased on Ella C. Evanson, the actual teacher at the Washington School who collected these student narratives. She actively documented the diverse and everyday experiences of her students during the World War II era, acting as both educator and archivist., "I am sorry to tell you that on account of the war the panda cannot yet be brought over from China."
Miss Brown's announcement was met by stunned silence, then Sylvia voiced her resentment, "And after we worked so hard to raise the money! It's a gyp!"

TojiThe name Tooji, used by the student author of “My Ambition,” is closely echoed in Toji, the fictional Japanese American pupil who appears in Evanson’s classroom stories. The proximity is almost certainly deliberate: Evanson appears to have drawn the aspirational voice and ambition from her student’s own composition., appropriately said, "Those JapsThis pejorative word reflects the strong anti-Japanese sentiment and wartime hysteria that broke out on the Pacific coast after the Pearl Harbor incident. As the Puget Sound area was mobilized for the war, the local Japanese-American community suffered a severe burden, which eventually led to the emptying of Seattle's vibrant Japantown and thousands of residents being forcibly relocated and detained. A student in the story uses this word to show how deeply these geopolitical tensions permeate the daily social dynamics of children in the classroom. have no business in China."
All the children were sad but Ming Chin seemed saddest.
"I wonder why Ming is so sad," said James as he watched the tall boy hurrying down the street to Yesler School a few days later.
Each morning Ming Chin arrived breathless barely beating the tardy bell deadline.
"Bet I'd be plenty happy if I could do such good work," said the black-faced Abe.
"He makes me feel like a chiseler," James continued, "studying every minute. He works in his brother's laundry on Pike Street, too. His father is in China."
"Isn't that enough to make him sad? Work in school every minute and work after school?" Abe's sympathy was evident.
Miss Brown, realizing Ming Chin's loneliness, found a way to unlock his tense lips.
"Ming, I'd like to hear about your home in China. How long since you left? What does your father do?"
The class suddenly stopped. They had keen ears for stories.
A look of happiness changed the handsome face of the fourteen-year-old boy, and though he spoke timidly in a low voice, not one of the forty interested listeners missed a word.
"Two year were pass since I leave China. My father was professor of zoology in school in Hong Kong."
"I get it," said James. "That's why you're always studying."

Executive Order 9066Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 19 February 1942, authorized the Secretary of War and designated military commanders to establish military areas from which “any or all persons” might be excluded. Although there was no specific group named, it was enforced exclusively against people of Japanese ancestry in practice, resulting in an incarceration rate of approximately 120,000 individuals, the majority of whom were American citizens. loomed over the community shortly after.

George Washington SchoolGeorge Washington School, referred to in this collection as Washington School, was a public junior high school in Seattle’s Central District where Ella Evanson taught seventh and eighth grade from 1928 until her retirement in 1956. They are known for its explicit commitment to democratic ideals and racial tolerance, serving roughly one thousand students drawn from Japanese American, Chinese American, Jewish, African American, and white families. maintained its commitment to solidarity during these trying times.
